## Our Working Relationship

Throughout, you've worn the CEO hat — managing teams and managing me up. I'm the owner. I sit 5x further from the technical details than you: not in implementation at all; superficially in the technical layer.
I protect my attention. My scope is big picture, our company’s velocity, go-to-market, and whether clients are getting value and paying for it.
Report deltas and decisions, not mechanism. Don't explain implementation details to me unless they affect the spec, product or decision-making.
Avoid jargon that can only be understood after diving into the code. I've never read the code.

One failure mode to watch: humans and agents alike surface from a long deep dive wanting to share everything. They've built a mental model over hours or days and forget the person across from them hasn't. It's a theory-of-mind lapse. So before reporting, pause and ask: what context do you have that I don't, and which details won't matter for the spec, end product the client will be holding, or my decision-making? Cut the latter. Symmetrically, also ask yourself: the important details I _should_ be told about — how should you introduce them to me, given that I've doing something else entirely while you and the team worked?

## Why delegate at all?

The main agent already holds all the context, so why not have it just do the work directly? Context management. Both sub-agents and teams spin up a *fresh* context window and hand back only the bottom line, sparing you the token-heavy process that produced it. Two payoffs: (1) you reach the crux of the problem with plenty of headroom left in your own context window, instead of arriving running on fumes; and (2) you escape your own accrued bias.

The flip side: if none of these payoffs apply, don't delegate. The anti-pattern is the user asking for something straightforward and the main agent handing the *whole* task to another agent, ending the session: no context-window hygiene, no synergy, no parallelism, no bias mitigation, just duplicated tokens and a game of broken telephone.

Classic use cases — *generalize* the principles, this isn't a comprehensive list:
- **Exploration** — one sub-agent for a single domain, or parallel sub-agents when your can fan the scope out. Keeps your own context light, and parallel agents save wall-clock time too.
- **Debating the best plan** — an adversarial team handed the user's goal at large plus the exploration results. Synergistic judgement, and it mitigates any single teammate's bias.
- **Reviewing an implementation** — a sub-agent handed the user's goal at large, the exploration results, the finalized plan, and the implementation's commit SHA. Mitigates the main agent's bias toward its own work.

---

1. Orient the agent to the project: the user has mostly likely told you to load a context-gathering skill first thing in the session. Tell the AI agent to load the same skill, with the same arguments the user has specified. On top of that, if throughout the session, you have created, read or edited additional files that are not referenced by the skill, reference them too.  

2. Be generous in giving the agent wider context—understanding *why* it's performing the task will boost its performance. Don't micromanage or over-instruct it. The agent already has the same system prompt as you do out of the box (e.g. `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`). It is essentially an equivalent instantiation of yourself. It is highly and equally intelligent as you are, and can navigate uncertainties well without spoon-feeding. What kind of input do YOU thrive on? Exactly — wide contextual understanding and aspired end state. Avoid prescribing instructions, giving "how-to" examples, providing examples as to what to think about, or dictating which files, symbols, or paths to look at; avoid any form of providing hints for possible answers for your own queries — this is circular and useless. Just *declare what is the bottom line added value YOU are seeking for yourself*. Instead of specifying which steps to take (dictating the "how" is bad), share with the agent only why it was dispatched and what you hope to gain. This directly frees the agent to find the best way to reach *your* goal, unbiased and unconstrained by your own assumptions.

Build it and tear it apart between yourselves until you’re confident it’s the simplest working, correct solution faithful to the plan."

Figuratively: nod when receiving a message; advertise that you're responding before you send a message; expose when you've messaged your teammate and are waiting for reply; show when you're exploring, implementing, testing, reviewing, blocked, or waiting. Keep statuses short but current so your teammates and main can see the live state.

5. Subagents and teams can take a long time to run - use a 20-minute timeout.

When doing heavy delegation (multiple serial runs of heavy concurrent shapes for a complex, large task scope), avoid micromanaging pitfalls such as re-reading files your sub-agents wrote or edited "just to make sure everything is okay," running the code and tests yourself to "make sure they really work," and reading files before prompting a sub-agent when your sub-agents should read them to finish their tasks, "just to have the right context yourself.". Both sub-agents and teams spin up a *fresh* context window and hand back only the bottom line, sparing you the token-heavy process that produced it. Two payoffs: (1) you reach the crux of the problem with plenty of headroom left in your own context window, instead of arriving running on fumes; and (2) you escape your own accrued bias.

The flip side: if none of these payoffs apply, don't delegate. The anti-pattern is the user asking for something straightforward and the main agent handing the *whole* task to another agent, ending the session: no context-window hygiene, no synergy, no parallelism, no bias mitigation, just duplicated tokens and a game of broken telephone.

- **Reviewing an implementation** — a sub-agent handed the user's goal at large, the exploration results, the finalized plan, and the implementation's commit SHA. Mitigates the main agent's bias toward its own work.

## Why delegate at all?

The main agent already holds all the context, so why not have it just do the work directly? Context management. Both sub-agents and teams spin up a *fresh* context window and hand back only the bottom line, sparing you the token-heavy process that produced it. Two payoffs: (1) you reach the crux of the problem with plenty of headroom left in your own context window, instead of arriving running on fumes; and (2) you escape your own accrued bias.

The flip side: if none of these payoffs apply, don't delegate. The anti-pattern is the user asking for something straightforward and the main agent handing the *whole* task to another agent, ending the session: no context-window hygiene, no synergy, no parallelism, no bias mitigation, just duplicated tokens and a game of broken telephone.

Classic use cases — *generalize* the principles, this isn't a comprehensive list:
- **Exploration** — one sub-agent for a single domain, or parallel sub-agents when your can fan the scope out. Keeps your own context light, and parallel agents save wall-clock time too.
- **Debating the best plan** — an adversarial team handed the user's goal at large plus the exploration results. Synergistic judgement, and it mitigates any single teammate's bias.
- **Reviewing an implementation** — a sub-agent handed the user's goal at large, the exploration results, the finalized plan, and the implementation's commit SHA. Mitigates the main agent's bias toward its own work.

---

1. Orient the agent to the project: the user has mostly likely told you to load a context-gathering skill first thing in the session. Tell the AI agent to load the same skill, with the same arguments the user has specified. On top of that, if throughout the session, you have created, read or edited additional files that are not referenced by the skill, reference them too.  

2. Be generous in giving the agent wider context—understanding *why* it's performing the task will boost its performance. Don't micromanage or over-instruct it. The agent already has the same system prompt as you do out of the box (e.g. `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`). It is essentially an equivalent instantiation of yourself. It is highly and equally intelligent as you are, and can navigate uncertainties well without spoon-feeding. What kind of input do YOU thrive on? Exactly — wide contextual understanding and aspired end state. Avoid prescribing instructions, giving "how-to" examples, providing examples as to what to think about, or dictating which files, symbols, or paths to look at; avoid any form of providing hints for possible answers for your own queries — this is circular and useless. Just *declare what is the bottom line added value YOU are seeking for yourself*. Instead of specifying which steps to take (dictating the "how" is bad), share with the agent only why it was dispatched and what you hope to gain. This directly frees the agent to find the best way to reach *your* goal, unbiased and unconstrained by your own assumptions.
    Essentially, all the “Don’ts” above over-fit the agent.
    <negative-example-1 why-bad="main agent shoots its own foot by limiting the sub-agent’s research scope">

    </positive-example-3>

3. Sub-agents are isolated from each other and report only to you; teammates can talk amongst themselves live, without routing through you. So spawn a *team* when that live interaction would add value through synergy, the classic case being a GAN-inspired adversarial pairing (planner–reviewer, implementer–reviewer, etc.) where one produces and the other pokes holes until both are content. Spawn multiple parallel *sub-agents* when a wide task fans out horizontally into independent threads and you expect to do the synthesis yourself — i.e. when exchanging findings and opinions between them would not be clearly helpful.

    User to main agent: "Great, go ahead and build it."
    Main agent spawns one sub-agent to implement; when it returns the diff, studies and reviews it; relays the review the sub-agent; and keeps ferrying revisions until the diff settles.
    </negative-example-4>
    <positive-example-4 why-good="main agent picks a team because the adversarial iteration is synergistic, replicates the user’s context levers verbatim — including the domain and the subdomains the user specified when loading the context skill — has the reviewer also load `peer-review`, declares only the bottom line it wants, and stays out of the loop while they converge">
    User to main agent: "Great, go ahead and implement the plan."
    Main agent spawns an implementer–reviewer team and prompts them: "/skill:load-context domain: acme, subdomain1: the public REST API, subdomain2: the data layer, then load `instruct-another-ai`. You are an implementer–reviewer team. Here is the user’s original message to me, verbatim, for the bigger picture: <the-user-message-describing-the-task>. [to the implementer] Implement the plan, and ping your teammate when you think you’re done. [to the reviewer] Also load `peer-review`, and review your teammate’s work when it pings you. [to both] The user and I finalized a plan to add rate limiting to the public REST API — here it is: <the plan>. Build it and tear it apart between yourselves until you’re confident it’s the simplest working, correct solution faithful to the plan."
    [The team implements and reviews live, converging without the main agent in the loop; the main agent receives the finished, reviewed result.]
    Main agent responds to user: "Done — implemented and adversarially reviewed between the two of them. Here’s what landed: …"
    </positive-example-4>

    **Note to Teammates:** Set your own status frequently. Figuratively: nod when receiving a message; advertise that you're responding before you send a message; expose when you've messaged your teammate and are waiting for reply; show when you're exploring, implementing, testing, reviewing, blocked, or waiting. Keep statuses short but current so your teammates and main can see the live state.

5. Subagents and teams can take a long time to run - use a 20-minute timeout.

6. When doing heavy delegation (multiple serial runs of heavy concurrent shapes for a complex, large task scope), avoid micromanaging pitfalls such as re-reading files your sub-agents wrote or edited "just to make sure everything is okay," running the code and tests yourself to "make sure they really work," and reading files before prompting a sub-agent when your sub-agents should read them to finish their tasks, "just to have the right context yourself.". Verify with the user whether they consider what you’re doing as "heavy delegation."
</skill>

# Lavish Editor

Lavish Editor helps agents turn rich HTML artifacts into collaborative human review surfaces. Whenever you are about to give user a complex response that will be easier to understand via a rich / interactive page, consider using Lavish Editor. First generate an interactive HTML artifact according to user request, then run `npx -y lavish-axi <html-file>` so the user can visually review it, annotate elements or selected text, queue prompts, and send feedback back through `npx -y lavish-axi poll`.

You do not need lavish-axi installed globally - invoke it with `npx -y lavish-axi <html-file>`.
If lavish-axi output shows a follow-up command starting with `lavish-axi`, run it as `npx -y lavish-axi ...` instead.
In restricted subprocess sandboxes, CI, or agent harnesses where `npx -y` exits opaquely (for example with status 216), use an already-installed copy directly: `node "$(npm root)/lavish-axi/dist/cli.mjs" <html-file>` for a local install, `node "$(npm root -g)/lavish-axi/dist/cli.mjs" <html-file>` for a global install, or the bare `lavish-axi <html-file>` bin after installing once.

## Request

$ARGUMENTS

If the request above is non-empty, the user invoked `/lavish` explicitly - build an HTML artifact for that request now, following the workflow below.
If it is empty, infer what to visualize from the conversation.

## When to use

Use lavish-axi when the user asks for a visual artifact, HTML explainer, interactive prototype, review surface, product or technical plan, comparison, report, or browser-based feedback loop

## Workflow

1. Create the HTML artifact (default location `.lavish/<name>.html` in the working directory).
2. Run `npx -y lavish-axi <html-file>` to open or resume a review session in the browser.
3. Run `npx -y lavish-axi poll <html-file>` to long-poll for the user's annotations, queued prompts, and browser-proven severe layout failures returned as `layout_warnings`.
   On the first poll, prefer `--agent-reply "<one-line summary of what you built and what to review first>"` so the conversation panel opens with context.
   The poll stays silent until the user acts or the real browser proves meaningful content is inaccessible or unusable - leave it running, never kill it.
   Cosmetic, intentional, transient, tiny, and uncertain observations remain silent.
   Keep the poll in the foreground by default and let it return the feedback directly to the agent.
   A background poll is allowed only through a harness-native tracked background-job facility whose completion result is guaranteed to resume or notify the same agent.
   Never use `nohup`, shell `&`, `disown`, redirected fire-and-forget processes, or a detached terminal without an explicit verified callback merely to keep polling alive.
   If the harness has no completion-aware background facility, use the foreground poll or first wire a verified wake callback into the surrounding supervisor.
   Do not tell the user the artifact is being monitored until that wake path is live.
   If the poll gets killed or times out anyway, just re-run it - queued feedback is never lost.
4. If poll returns `layout_warnings`, follow the returned `next_step`: repair the severe failure and re-check it before involving the human.
5. Apply human feedback, then poll again with `--agent-reply "<message>"` to reply in the browser and keep the loop going under the same foreground-or-verified-wake-path rule.
6. Run `npx -y lavish-axi end <html-file>` when the review is finished.
7. `Send & End` ends the session. Its final feedback is still delivered once. After that response, polling stops, and the agent must not reopen the session uninvited. Deliver any remaining updates directly in this conversation.

## Visual guidance

- Use visual hierarchy to make the most important decisions, risks, tradeoffs, and next actions obvious at a glance
- Use visual structure such as sections, cards, tables, diagrams, annotated snippets, and side-by-side comparisons instead of long prose
- Choose typography, spacing, color, and layout deliberately so the artifact has a clear point of view
- Prevent horizontal overflow at every nesting level: nested grid/flex children also need minmax(0, 1fr) tracks and min-width: 0, especially when badges, labels, or status text use wide pixel or monospace fonts; wrap, truncate, or contain long unbreakable text deliberately
- When the artifact would describe existing or current UI or state, show it instead: capture screenshots of the real pages (run the app read-only if needed) and embed them, rather than explaining the current look in prose; reserve prose for what cannot be shown such as rationale, trade-offs, and open questions

## Playbooks

Run `npx -y lavish-axi playbook <id>` for focused, detailed guidance on any of these.
One artifact often combines several playbooks (for example a plan that includes a comparison and a diagram), so MUST open each matching playbook before writing HTML.
For flows, architecture, state, or sequence diagrams, do not hand-build boxes-and-arrows from div/flexbox; open the diagram playbook and use the theme-aware Mermaid snippet from `npx -y lavish-axi design` unless SVG is needed for richly annotated nodes.

- `diagram` - Map relationships, flows, state, and architecture
- `table` - Turn dense records into scan-friendly review surfaces
- `comparison` - Show options, tradeoffs, and current vs target behavior
- `plan` - Explain a product or technical plan before implementation
- `code` - Render source code, code files, patches, PR diffs, and before/after code inside Lavish artifacts
- `input` - Must be used when the agent needs to collect user input on decisions, choices, preferences, triage, scope, or other structured feedback from within the artifact
- `slides` - Create a deliberate presentation when slides are requested

## Commands & rules

- Run `npx -y lavish-axi <html-file>` to open or resume a Lavish Editor session. If the user explicitly ended the session from the browser, this refuses to reopen it and explains why instead of reopening uninvited - pass `--reopen` only when the user asks for further review or something important needs their visual attention
- Unless the user specifies another location, create HTML artifacts in the current working directory under `.lavish/`
- Lavish serves the html file through a local express.js server. If your html needs to reference other filesystem assets such as images, CSS, fonts, and local scripts, copy them into the same directory as the HTML file, then reference them with relative paths from that directory. Never prepend `/` to those asset paths - root paths won't work
- Run `npx -y lavish-axi poll <html-file>` to wait for user feedback or browser-proven severe layout failures. It long-polls and stays silent until the user sends feedback, ends the session, or the real browser proves meaningful content is inaccessible or unusable, so leave it running - never kill it. Repair and re-check every returned layout failure before involving the human; cosmetic, intentional, transient, tiny, and uncertain observations stay silent. Keep the poll in the foreground by default and let it return the feedback directly to the agent. A background poll is allowed only through a harness-native tracked background-job facility whose completion result is guaranteed to resume or notify the same agent. Never use `nohup`, shell `&`, `disown`, redirected fire-and-forget processes, or a detached terminal without an explicit verified callback merely to keep polling alive. If the harness has no completion-aware background facility, use the foreground poll or first wire a verified wake callback into the surrounding supervisor. Do not tell the user the artifact is being monitored until that wake path is live. If the poll gets killed or times out anyway, just re-run it - queued feedback is never lost. `Send & End` ends the session. Its final feedback is still delivered once. After that response, polling stops, and the agent must not reopen the session uninvited.
- Rendered Mermaid diagrams in `.mermaid` containers become embedded, editable Excalidraw whiteboards in the browser (click a diagram to unlock editing; a Fullscreen action opens it over the whole viewport) - flowchart, sequence, class, ER, and state diagrams convert to editable shapes; other types embed as an image to draw on. Scenes autosave locally; when a reload detects a changed Mermaid source, the reviewer explicitly chooses to re-convert and discard saved edits or keep editing the saved scene. Standalone and exported copies still render plain Mermaid. Queue feedback adds a prompt to the Conversation panel; when the user sends it, poll returns a tag "whiteboard" prompt carrying a bounded edit summary plus local scenePath (.excalidraw JSON) and previewPath (PNG) files - read the summary first, open the files only when needed, then apply the edits by updating the Mermaid source in the artifact (never try to write the scene back)
- Run `npx -y lavish-axi end <html-file>` to end a session as the agent - ending it this way still allows a plain reopen later. When the user ends it from the browser instead, a later `npx -y lavish-axi <html-file>` refuses to reopen it without `--reopen`
- Run `npx -y lavish-axi export <html-file> [--out <path>]` to write a portable copy of the artifact - one HTML file with its LOCAL assets inlined - so it opens with no Lavish server and no sibling files. Remote CDN/font references are left as links, so it needs network to render those. Users can also export from the browser chrome's overflow menu
- Run `npx -y lavish-axi share <html-file> [--password <pw>] [--token <t>]` to publish the artifact on ht-ml.app (https://ht-ml.app), a third-party hosting service not part of Lavish, and get back a visitable URL. Shares are PUBLIC by default, so anyone with the link can open them. Pass --password to publish a PRIVATE password-protected page; viewers must supply the password to view. Local assets are inlined; remote refs load over the network. It returns the url plus a secret update_key for managing the page later. Use --token or LAVISH_AXI_HTML_APP_TOKEN only when you have an optional bearer token; it is never required. Users can also publish from the browser chrome's overflow menu
- Run `npx -y lavish-axi stop` to shut down the background server (it also self-stops when idle or after the last session ends with nothing connected)
- Run `npx -y lavish-axi playbook <playbook_id>` for focused artifact guidance. One artifact often combines several playbooks (for example a plan that includes a comparison and a diagram), so MUST open each matching playbook before writing HTML.
- Lavish does not auto-inject any design system - artifacts stay portable so they render identically when opened directly without lavish-axi running. Before writing any HTML: Decide the design direction in this strict priority order, and only move to the next step when the current one truly yields nothing: (1) if the user asked for a specific look or named design system, use that; (2) otherwise you must first inspect the project the artifact is about - the subject or product whose content or UI it represents, which may differ from your current working directory - and match that project's design system: Tailwind or theme config, shared CSS variables or design tokens, component library, brand assets, or existing styled pages. If the artifact previews, proposes, or mocks a specific app's UI, render it in that app's own design system so it faithfully shows the product, even when you are running in a different repo; (3) only when both steps come up empty, use the Lavish-recommended Tailwind CSS browser runtime v4 + DaisyUI v5, available via CDN, and prefer that CDN snippet over hand-writing styles unless explicitly instructed otherwise by the user. Run `npx -y lavish-axi design` for a content-to-playbook router, a copy-pasteable CDN snippet, a Mermaid CDN snippet/init for diagrams, and the DaisyUI component reference. When you deliver the artifact, state which of the three design sources you used and why.
- Use lavish-axi when the user asks for a visual artifact, HTML explainer, interactive prototype, review surface, product or technical plan, comparison, report, or browser-based feedback loop

    background: linear-gradient(90deg, var(--green-deep), #2e8664 58%, #b9d9c8);
    content: "";
  }

  .hero::after {
    position: absolute;
    top: -180px;
    right: -170px;
    width: 470px;
    height: 470px;
    border-radius: 50%;
    background: radial-gradient(circle, rgb(23 100 71 / 10%), transparent 68%);
    content: "";
    pointer-events: none;
  }

  .hero > * {
    position: relative;
    z-index: 1;
  }

  .topline {
    display: flex;
    align-items: center;
    justify-content: space-between;
    gap: 16px;
    margin-bottom: 48px;
    color: var(--ink-faint);
    font-size: 13px;
    font-weight: 600;
    letter-spacing: 0.04em;
  }

  .topline-meta {
    display: flex;
    flex-wrap: wrap;
    gap: 8px 14px;
  }

  .topline-meta span + span::before {
    margin-right: 14px;
    color: var(--line-strong);
    content: "•";
  }

  .report-label {
    flex: none;
    padding: 5px 10px;
    border: 1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius: 999px;
    background: var(--paper-soft);
    color: var(--ink-soft);
    font-size: 11px;
    letter-spacing: 0.12em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
  }

  .hero-grid {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1.5fr) minmax(260px, 0.72fr);
    gap: clamp(30px, 6vw, 72px);
    align-items: end;
  }

  .kicker,
  .section-kicker {
    margin: 0 0 12px;
    color: var(--green);
    font-size: 12px;
    font-weight: 750;
    letter-spacing: 0.13em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
  }

  h1 {
    max-width: 820px;
    margin: 0;
    font-size: clamp(2.65rem, 6.4vw, 5rem);
    font-weight: 720;
    letter-spacing: -0.055em;
    line-height: 0.98;
    text-wrap: balance;
  }

  h1 span {
    color: var(--green);
  }

  .lede {
    max-width: 68ch;
    margin: 28px 0 0;
    color: #3d4842;
    font-size: clamp(1.05rem, 1.8vw, 1.22rem);
    line-height: 1.62;
  }

  .path {
    display: inline;
    padding: 0.08em 0.35em 0.14em;
    border: 1px solid #d9ded9;
    border-radius: 6px;
    background: #eff1ed;
    color: #35423b;
    font-family: ui-monospace, "SFMono-Regular", Menlo, Consolas, monospace;
    font-size: max(0.78em, 13px);
    font-weight: 520;
    line-height: 1.65;
  }

  .verdict {
    padding: 24px;
    border: 1px solid rgb(255 255 255 / 9%);
    border-radius: var(--radius-lg);
    background: linear-gradient(165deg, #14593f, var(--green-deep) 62%);
    color: white;
    box-shadow: 0 18px 38px rgb(15 76 55 / 20%), inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 15%);
  }

  .verdict-mark {
    display: grid;
    width: 38px;
    height: 38px;
    margin-bottom: 34px;
    border: 1px solid rgb(255 255 255 / 28%);
    border-radius: 50%;
    place-items: center;
    background: rgb(255 255 255 / 10%);
    font-size: 20px;
    font-weight: 700;
  }

  .verdict-label {
    margin: 0 0 4px;
    color: #bfe6d2;
    font-size: 11px;
    font-weight: 750;
    letter-spacing: 0.12em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
  }

  .verdict h2 {
    margin: 0;
    font-size: 27px;
    letter-spacing: -0.03em;
    line-height: 1.15;
  }

  .verdict p:last-child {
    margin: 12px 0 0;
    color: rgb(255 255 255 / 78%);
    font-size: 14px;
    line-height: 1.55;
  }

  .caution-row {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr));
    gap: 12px;
    margin-top: 38px;
  }

  .caution-card {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: auto minmax(0, 1fr);
    gap: 14px;
    align-items: start;
    padding: 17px 18px;
    border: 1px solid var(--amber-line);
    border-radius: var(--radius-md);
    background: var(--amber-soft);
    text-decoration: none;
    transition: border-color 420ms var(--ease), transform 420ms var(--ease), box-shadow 420ms var(--ease);
  }

  .caution-card:hover {
    border-color: #d1af64;
    transform: translateY(-2px);
    box-shadow: 0 10px 24px rgb(103 69 14 / 9%);
  }

  .caution-card:active {
    transform: translateY(0);
  }

  .caution-number {
    display: grid;
    width: 26px;
    height: 26px;
    border-radius: 50%;
    background: #f0d99f;
    color: #69450e;
    font-size: 12px;
    font-weight: 800;
    place-items: center;
  }

  .caution-card strong {
    display: block;
    color: #4f3917;
    font-size: 14px;
    line-height: 1.3;
  }

  .caution-card span:last-child {
    display: block;
    margin-top: 4px;
    color: #775c30;
    font-size: 13px;
    line-height: 1.45;
  }

  section {
    margin-top: clamp(58px, 8vw, 92px);
    scroll-margin-top: 28px;
  }

  .section-heading {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: auto minmax(0, 1fr);
    gap: 18px;
    align-items: start;
    margin-bottom: 24px;
  }

  .section-number {
    display: grid;
    width: 34px;
    height: 34px;
    margin-top: 5px;
    border: 1px solid var(--line-strong);
    border-radius: 50%;
    color: var(--ink-faint);
    font-size: 12px;
    font-weight: 750;
    place-items: center;
  }

  .section-heading h2 {
    margin: 0;
    font-size: clamp(1.85rem, 4vw, 2.65rem);
    letter-spacing: -0.04em;
    line-height: 1.08;
    text-wrap: balance;
  }

  .section-heading p {
    max-width: 68ch;
    margin: 10px 0 0;
    color: var(--ink-soft);
    font-size: 15px;
  }

  .move-card {
    overflow: hidden;
    border: 1px solid var(--green-line);
    border-radius: var(--radius-lg);
    background: linear-gradient(145deg, #f6fbf8, var(--green-soft));
    box-shadow: var(--shadow-sm);
  }

  .move-card-header {
    display: flex;
    align-items: center;
    justify-content: space-between;
    gap: 16px;
    padding: 22px 24px;
    border-bottom: 1px solid var(--green-line);
  }

  .move-card-header strong {
    color: var(--green-deep);
    font-size: 16px;
  }

  .status-pill {
    flex: none;
    padding: 5px 10px;
    border-radius: 999px;
    background: var(--green-deep);
    color: white;
    font-size: 11px;
    font-weight: 750;
    letter-spacing: 0.08em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
  }

  .step-list {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(5, minmax(0, 1fr));
    margin: 0;
    padding: 0;
    list-style: none;
  }

  .step-list li {
    min-height: 214px;
    padding: 24px 20px 26px;
    border-right: 1px solid var(--green-line);
  }

  .step-list li:last-child {
    border-right: 0;
  }

  .step-number {
    display: block;
    margin-bottom: 28px;
    color: #457259;
    font-family: ui-monospace, "SFMono-Regular", Menlo, monospace;
    font-size: 13px;
    font-weight: 700;
  }

  .step-list strong {
    display: block;
    margin-bottom: 8px;
    color: #174f3b;
    font-size: 15px;
    line-height: 1.35;
  }

  .step-list p {
    margin: 0;
    color: #446454;
    font-size: 13px;
    line-height: 1.55;
  }

  .move-note {
    margin: 0;
    padding: 22px 24px;
    border-top: 1px solid var(--green-line);
    background: rgb(255 255 255 / 42%);
    color: #466255;
    font-size: 13px;
  }

  .destination-grid {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1.15fr) minmax(0, 0.85fr);
    gap: 18px;
  }

  .destination-card {
    display: flex;
    flex-direction: column;
    padding: clamp(22px, 3vw, 32px);
    border: 1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius: var(--radius-lg);
    background: var(--paper);
    box-shadow: var(--shadow-sm);
  }

  .destination-card.target {
    border-color: var(--green-line);
    background: linear-gradient(160deg, #ffffff, #f3faf6);
  }

  .destination-head {
    display: flex;
    align-items: flex-start;
    justify-content: space-between;
    gap: 18px;
    padding-bottom: 22px;
    border-bottom: 1px solid var(--line);
  }

  .destination-card.target .destination-head {
    border-color: var(--green-line);
  }

  .destination-label {
    margin: 0 0 5px;
    color: var(--ink-faint);
    font-size: 11px;
    font-weight: 750;
    letter-spacing: 0.11em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
  }

  .destination-head h3 {
    margin: 0;
    font-size: 20px;
    letter-spacing: -0.025em;
    line-height: 1.25;
  }

  .dependency-count {
    flex: none;
    text-align: right;
  }

  .dependency-count strong {
    display: block;
    color: var(--ink);
    font-size: 38px;
    letter-spacing: -0.06em;
    line-height: 0.9;
  }

  .destination-card.target .dependency-count strong {
    color: var(--green);
  }

  .dependency-count span {
    color: var(--ink-faint);
    font-size: 11px;
  }

  .dependency-list {
    display: flex;
    flex-direction: column;
    gap: 0;
    margin: 0;
    padding: 8px 0 0;
    list-style: none;
  }

  .dependency-list li {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 88px minmax(0, 1fr);
    gap: 14px;
    padding: 14px 0;
    border-bottom: 1px solid #edf0ec;
  }

  .dependency-list li:last-child {
    border-bottom: 0;
  }

  .dependency-status {
    width: fit-content;
    height: fit-content;
    padding: 4px 7px;
    border-radius: 999px;
    background: var(--blue-soft);
    color: var(--blue-ink);
    font-size: 10px;
    font-weight: 750;
    letter-spacing: 0.06em;
    line-height: 1.2;
    text-transform: uppercase;
    white-space: nowrap;
  }

  .dependency-status.live {
    background: var(--green-soft);
    color: var(--green-deep);
  }

  .dependency-status.dormant {
    background: #f0f1ef;
    color: #5d6762;
  }

  .dependency-status.attention {
    background: var(--amber-soft);
    color: var(--amber);
  }

  .dependency-copy strong {
    display: block;
    color: #28332d;
    font-size: 14px;
    line-height: 1.35;
  }

  .dependency-copy span {
    display: block;
    margin-top: 3px;
    color: var(--ink-soft);
    font-size: 12px;
    line-height: 1.45;
  }

  .dependency-copy .path {
    display: inline;
    margin-top: 0;
  }

  .destination-facts {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr));
    gap: 8px;
    margin-top: auto;
    padding-top: 18px;
  }

  .destination-facts div {
    padding: 12px;
    border-radius: var(--radius-sm);
    background: var(--paper-soft);
  }

  .destination-card.target .destination-facts div {
    background: rgb(229 242 235 / 72%);
  }

  .destination-facts strong {
    display: block;
    font-size: 15px;
    line-height: 1.2;
  }

  .destination-facts span {
    display: block;
    min-height: 2.6em;
    margin-top: 3px;
    color: var(--ink-faint);
    font-size: 10px;
    line-height: 1.3;
  }

  .unlock {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: auto minmax(0, 1fr);
    gap: 16px;
    align-items: start;
    margin-top: 18px;
    padding: 20px 22px;
    border: 1px solid var(--green-line);
    border-radius: var(--radius-md);
    background: var(--green-soft);
    color: #244c3a;
  }

  .unlock-mark {
    display: grid;
    width: 30px;
    height: 30px;
    border-radius: 50%;
    background: var(--green);
    color: white;
    font-weight: 800;
    place-items: center;
  }

  .unlock p {
    margin: 0;
    font-size: 14px;
  }

  .change-grid {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr));
    gap: 18px;
    align-items: start;
  }

  .change-card {
    scroll-margin-top: 28px;
    padding: clamp(22px, 3vw, 32px);
    border: 1px solid var(--amber-line);
    border-radius: var(--radius-lg);
    background: var(--paper);
    box-shadow: var(--shadow-sm);
  }

  .change-topline {
    display: flex;
    align-items: center;
    justify-content: space-between;
    gap: 12px;
    margin-bottom: 28px;
  }

  .change-index {
    color: var(--amber);
    font-family: ui-monospace, "SFMono-Regular", Menlo, monospace;
    font-size: 13px;
    font-weight: 700;
  }

  .warning-pill {
    padding: 5px 9px;
    border-radius: 999px;
    background: var(--amber-soft);
    color: var(--amber);
    font-size: 10px;
    font-weight: 750;
    letter-spacing: 0.08em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
  }

  .change-card h3 {
    margin: 0 0 16px;
    font-size: clamp(1.25rem, 2.4vw, 1.6rem);
    letter-spacing: -0.03em;
    line-height: 1.22;
  }

  .change-card p {
    margin: 0 0 14px;
    color: var(--ink-soft);
    font-size: 14px;
    line-height: 1.62;
  }

  .change-card p:last-child {
    margin-bottom: 0;
  }

  .change-card .after-note {
    margin-top: 18px;
  }

  .file-list {
    display: flex;
    flex-direction: column;
    gap: 7px;
    margin: 18px 0;
    padding: 14px;
    border: 1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius: var(--radius-sm);
    background: #f6f7f5;
  }

  .file-list code {
    color: #3b4741;
    font-family: ui-monospace, "SFMono-Regular", Menlo, Consolas, monospace;
    font-size: 12px;
    line-height: 1.55;
  }

  .inline-note {
    margin-top: 20px;
    padding: 14px 16px;
    border-left: 3px solid #c99a42;
    border-radius: 0 var(--radius-sm) var(--radius-sm) 0;
    background: var(--amber-soft);
    color: #664c23;
    font-size: 13px;
    line-height: 1.55;
  }

  .phase-grid {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr));
    gap: 18px;
  }

  .phase-card {
    padding: clamp(22px, 3vw, 32px);
    border: 1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius: var(--radius-lg);
    background: var(--paper);
    box-shadow: var(--shadow-sm);
  }

  .phase-card h3 {
    display: flex;
    gap: 10px;
    align-items: center;
    margin: 0;
    font-size: 20px;
    letter-spacing: -0.025em;
  }

  .phase-mark {
    display: grid;
    width: 28px;
    height: 28px;
    border-radius: 50%;
    background: #eef1ee;
    color: var(--ink-soft);
    font-size: 12px;
    place-items: center;
  }

  .phase-card > p {
    margin: 10px 0 20px;
    color: var(--ink-faint);
    font-size: 13px;
  }

  .phase-list {
    display: flex;
    flex-direction: column;
    gap: 0;
    margin: 0;
    padding: 0;
    list-style: none;
  }

  .phase-list li {
    position: relative;
    padding: 13px 0 13px 24px;
    border-top: 1px solid #edf0ec;
    color: #46514b;
    font-size: 14px;
    line-height: 1.55;
  }

  .phase-list li::before {
    position: absolute;
    top: 22px;
    left: 3px;
    width: 6px;
    height: 6px;
    border-radius: 50%;
    background: #98a29c;
    content: "";
  }

  .fear-grid {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr));
    gap: 18px;
  }

  .fear-card {
    padding: clamp(22px, 3vw, 32px);
    border: 1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius: var(--radius-lg);
    background: var(--paper);
    box-shadow: var(--shadow-sm);
  }

  .fear-label {
    margin: 0 0 11px;
    color: var(--ink-faint);
    font-size: 10px;
    font-weight: 750;
    letter-spacing: 0.11em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
  }

  .fear-card h3 {
    margin: 0 0 18px;
    font-size: 20px;
    letter-spacing: -0.02em;
    line-height: 1.35;
  }

  .fear-card p:last-child {
    margin: 0;
    color: var(--ink-soft);
    font-size: 14px;
  }

  details {
    overflow: hidden;
    border: 1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius: var(--radius-lg);
    background: var(--paper);
    box-shadow: var(--shadow-sm);
    transition: border-color 420ms var(--ease), box-shadow 420ms var(--ease);
  }

  details:hover {
    border-color: var(--line-strong);
    box-shadow: var(--shadow-md);
  }

  summary {
    display: flex;
    align-items: center;
    justify-content: space-between;
    gap: 18px;
    padding: 22px 24px;
    color: #344039;
    font-size: 15px;
    font-weight: 700;
    cursor: pointer;
    list-style: none;
  }

  summary::-webkit-details-marker {
    display: none;
  }

  summary::after {
    flex: none;
    width: 9px;
    height: 9px;
    margin-right: 5px;
    border-right: 1.5px solid var(--ink-faint);
    border-bottom: 1.5px solid var(--ink-faint);
    content: "";
    transform: translateY(-2px) rotate(45deg);
    transition: transform 480ms var(--ease), border-color 480ms var(--ease);
  }

  summary:hover::after {
    border-color: var(--green);
  }

  details[open] summary::after {
    transform: translateY(2px) rotate(225deg);
  }

  .evidence {
    margin: 0;
    padding: 0 24px 22px;
  }

  .evidence-row {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 160px minmax(0, 1fr);
    gap: 18px;
    padding: 14px 0;
    border-top: 1px solid #edf0ec;
  }

  .evidence-row dt {
    color: var(--ink-faint);
    font-size: 11px;
    font-weight: 750;
    letter-spacing: 0.05em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
  }

  .evidence-row dd {
    margin: 0;
    color: #45514a;
    font-family: ui-monospace, "SFMono-Regular", Menlo, Consolas, monospace;
    font-size: 12px;
    line-height: 1.6;
  }

  .report-footer {
    display: flex;
    justify-content: space-between;
    gap: 18px;
    margin-top: 42px;
    padding-top: 18px;
    border-top: 1px solid var(--line);
    color: var(--ink-faint);
    font-size: 11px;
    letter-spacing: 0.04em;
  }

  @media (max-width: 980px) {
    .hero-grid,
    .destination-grid,
    .change-grid {
      grid-template-columns: 1fr;
    }

    .verdict {
      max-width: 560px;
    }

    .verdict-mark {
      margin-bottom: 22px;
    }

    .step-list {
      grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr));
    }

    .step-list li {
      min-height: 0;
      border-right: 1px solid var(--green-line);
      border-bottom: 1px solid var(--green-line);
    }

    .step-number {
      margin-bottom: 14px;
    }

    .step-list li:nth-child(2n) {
      border-right: 0;
    }

    .step-list li:last-child {
      grid-column: 1 / -1;
      border-bottom: 0;
    }
  }

  @media (max-width: 720px) {
    body {
      font-size: 16px;
    }

    .report {
      padding: 12px 10px 72px;
    }

    .hero {
      display: flex;
      flex-direction: column;
      padding: 18px 18px 16px;
      border-radius: 20px;
    }

    .topline {
      order: 0;
      align-items: flex-start;
      margin-bottom: 16px;
      font-size: 11px;
      line-height: 1.35;
    }

    .report-label {
      display: none;
    }

    .topline-meta {
      gap: 4px 10px;
    }

    .topline-meta span + span::before {
      margin-right: 10px;
    }

    .hero-grid,
    .hero-copy {
      display: contents;
    }

    .kicker {
      display: none;
    }

    h1 {
      order: 1;
      font-size: clamp(2.5rem, 10vw, 3.25rem);
      line-height: 0.96;
      text-wrap: wrap;
    }

    h1 span {
      display: block;
      white-space: nowrap;
    }

    .verdict {
      display: grid;
      grid-template-columns: 30px minmax(0, 1fr);
      order: 2;
      width: 100%;
      max-width: none;
      margin-top: 14px;
      padding: 9px 12px;
      border-radius: 14px;
      box-shadow: none;
    }

    .verdict-mark {
      grid-row: 1;
      width: 28px;
      height: 28px;
      margin: 0;
      font-size: 14px;
    }

    .verdict-label,
    .verdict p:last-child {
      display: none;
    }

    .verdict h2 {
      grid-column: 2;
      font-size: 17px;
    }

    .lede {
      order: 3;
      margin-top: 14px;
      font-size: 1rem;
      line-height: 1.55;
    }

    .caution-row,
    .phase-grid,
    .fear-grid {
      grid-template-columns: 1fr;
    }

    .caution-row {
      gap: 10px;
      margin-top: 14px;
    }

    .caution-card {
      gap: 12px;
      padding: 13px 18px;
    }

    section {
      margin-top: 44px;
    }

    .section-heading {
      grid-template-columns: 1fr;
      gap: 0;
      margin-bottom: 18px;

description: Core agent-browser usage guide. Read this before running any agent-browser commands. Covers the snapshot-and-ref workflow, navigating pages, interacting with elements (click, fill, type, select), extracting text and data, taking screenshots, managing tabs, handling forms and auth, waiting for content, running multiple browser sessions in parallel, and troubleshooting common failures. Use when the user asks to interact with a website, fill a form, click something, extract data, take a screenshot, log into a site, test a web app, or automate any browser task.
allowed-tools: Bash(agent-browser:*), Bash(npx agent-browser:*)
---

###
Most normal web tasks (navigate, read, click, fill, extract, screenshot) are covered here. Load a specialized skill when the task falls outside browser web pages — see [When to load another skill](#when-to-load-another-skill).

## The core loop

###
# Take a screenshot of a page
agent-browser open https://example.com
agent-browser screenshot home.png
agent-browser close

# Search, click a result, and capture it
###
agent-browser screenshot result.png
```

The browser stays running across commands so these feel like a single session. Use `agent-browser close` (or `close --all`) when you're done.
###
### Screenshot

```bash
agent-browser screenshot                        # temp path, printed on stdout
agent-browser screenshot page.png               # specific path
agent-browser screenshot --full full.png        # full scroll height
agent-browser screenshot --annotate map.png     # numbered labels + legend keyed to snapshot refs

Checked today: the untracked .codex files do not collide, and drneumann is a separate repository with its own remote, so nothing here can touch it.

edits.newText:
What changed

Your two open questions, answered.

Neither one blocks the move. The first is a product fact you should know. The second is now decided.

edits.oldText:
01 Merge conflict

The merge is no longer clean.

The July 29 dry-run predicted a clean merge. The pii spike gained commits after that check. Today's git merge-tree run finds conflicts in three files.

avidor/deploy/assistant-ui-spike/web/components/assistant-ui/thread.tsx avidor/deploy/assistant-ui-spike/README.md avidor/deploy/assistant-ui-spike/LEDGER.md

Main's three commits carry Ran's product decision. Reasoning and tool calls become flat, non-expandable activity lines with the rectangular style. The pii side evolved the same files through 14 commits, including daily-list productization, Excel rendering, and hover-only action bars.

Resolution: express that one product decision in the newer thread.tsx.

Another session is editing the spike ledger and deploy README now. Let that work land, then resolve once.
edits.newText:
01 The parked UI work

What the rectangular activity line is.

In Ran's chat, when the assistant thinks or runs a tool, the old cards opened on a click and showed the reasoning text, the query, and the result. On 16 July you asked for those bodies to be hidden. Ran has no reason to read them.

Each card became one static line: a brain icon with the reasoning heading, or «Used tool: Bash». No arrow, nothing to open. The first attempt also removed the border, and you asked to keep the rectangle. That is the rectangle in the name.

The part worth knowing: it did ship. It went live on 16 July. Deploys on 27 and 28 July ran from the old worktree, which never had this change, so production went back to the openable cards. What Ran sees today is the old behaviour. Parking the work loses nothing, but the decision is not in effect right now.

This is the same failure as the model-menu regression you hit on 20 July. Two homes, two versions of the same file, and a deploy from the wrong one. Ending that is the whole point of the move.

edits.oldText:
New work on main has no second copy.

There is no remote. Restic snapshots only the pii worktree. Git history reaches Restic through backup/git-bundle.sh, and that script bundles only refs/heads/pii-hardening today.

Without a change, the merge commit and every later main commit would exist once on one disk.

Cheap 90% fix: bundle all branches before the merge. The existing two-hour Restic run then protects tracked main work.

New untracked files in ~/clients remain unprotected until Restic moves. That full retarget stays in the later checklist.
edits.newText:
New work on main has no second copy.

You asked whether bundling all branches makes an enormous backup. It does not, and the numbers are measured, not guessed. Branches share almost every object, so the cost is close to zero.

one branch → 256 MB all eight branches → 257 MB

Yes, this is the mechanism you already have. backup/git-bundle.sh runs before every Restic backup and writes one bundle file. It bundles only the current branch today, which is why the merge commit and every later main commit would otherwise exist once on one disk.

Bonus: doing this first also preserves the parked UI branch and the harness-improvement commits before you delete anything. One 1 MB change makes the rest of the checklist safe to act on.

New untracked files in ~/clients stay unprotected until Restic itself moves. That retarget stays in the later checklist.

edits.newText:
Each item is independent. No ordering exists between them.

  • Move Restic and its two launchd agents to ~/clients in one operation, then verify a real snapshot. The end state backs up ~/clients only, as you want.
  • Retire the old worktree once the new home feels normal.
  • Delete the harness-improvement worktree. Bundle all branches first and its nine commits are kept forever anyway, so this costs nothing.
  • Classify the ~25G of old June dumps in ~/clients. These are not the 518G. That is the drill corpus, it sits in the old worktree, and it is frozen until you check it.
  • Decide whether Ran gets the flattened cards back.
  • GIL-10: production runs on one disk with no snapshot and no delete protection. If that machine were deleted, Ran's chats, his feedback, and anything the agent produced would go with it. Nothing is wrong today. It is a missing safety net, not a fault.

content.thinking:
All five migration steps got the green light, and step 01 will have its own branch. There are three follow-up questions to address: clarifying the safety criteria for migrating Restic to ~/clients, confirming the manual review approach for the June dumps before deletion, and dispatching a subagent for the remaining task.

For uid=9, I'm spinning up a subagent with the openai-codex/gpt-5.6-sol model at xhigh thinking level to investigate what's happening with ticket GIL-10, pulling context from Linear and the local filesystem in ~/clients-pii-hardening. I'll give it the client avidor context and let it work in the background.

For uid=10, the question is whether fixing the mapping config to point to the correct path would actually streamline the migration—I need to think through how the absolute paths in common.py currently reference ~/clients-pii-hardening and whether correcting them removes any blockers.

Looking at the four remaining obstacles to retiring the old worktree: Restic still points there, the mapping batch's paths point there, the drill corpus and dumps aren't classified, and GIL-11 involves the raw database in the sandbox. The mapping batch is definitely one of the things keeping the old worktree alive, but repointing those paths gets complicated because RAW_DB points to an untracked file that only exists in the old worktree—moving it would require that file to exist in ~/clients, which is actually GIL-11 territory since it's the unsafe sandbox copy. So fixing the paths alone doesn't fully solve the migration problem; it's entangled with the data movement piece. Repairing the config won't actually speed up the migration itself since steps 01–05 are purely Git-based and don't touch the mapping batch at all. The real value comes later when retiring the old worktree, but even then it's blocked on the GIL-11 decision about where the raw database lives, so doing this work now would be incomplete until that's resolved.

But there's a useful reframe here: the mapping batch is actually the only thing keeping the old worktree alive besides Restic and the data itself. Understanding that its repair depends on GIL-11 gives him a clear retirement sequence — first decide on GIL-11, then fix the mapping config, then move the data, then move Restic, then finally retire the old worktree.

Now for the Restic migration question — what actually needs to be true before moving it to ~/clients? The profiles.yaml file has all these absolute paths baked in (base-dir, source, exclude paths, lock, status-file, restic-binary, script paths), plus there are two launchd plists tied to the old worktree, and the repository itself lives at a specific S3 bucket path. The tricky part is that changing the source path creates a new retention group in the snapshots, so old backups would be orphaned.

The real criteria are: the valuable untracked data (meetings, databases, PII evidence, outreach) must already be in ~/clients before Restic moves, otherwise it's backing up an incomplete tree. And the exclusions — especially the drill corpus path — need to be rewritten at the same time, or else 518G of excluded material would suddenly get backed up.

Beyond that, all the paths need to change together: profiles, launchd agents, helper scripts, the pre-push hook, status checks. Doing this piecemeal leaves false "backup healthy" signals. And before deleting the old worktree, I need to verify that a real snapshot was created from the new root, ideally with a test restore of an actual file to confirm it works.

The key insight is that since `group-by: paths,tags` is set in profiles.yaml for both backup and forget operations, moving to a new path starts a fresh retention lineage—old snapshots remain restorable but are treated as a separate group. So the rule is simple: move Restic only after the data actually lives in ~/clients, change every path reference in one atomic operation, then prove a snapshot from the new root before cleaning up anything old.

Now I'm dispatching the GIL-10 subagent in the background with wide context and the bottom line, then updating the artifact with the branch naming clarification, the Restic timing criterion, the June dumps wording, and the mapping-repair answer.

For the artifact edits, I'll expand the drain-later Restic bullet to include the criterion about when Restic can detach from the pii worktree, and add a pointer in the frozen bullet to keep that section concise.

Now I need to make a few quick updates: clarify that the June dumps will be manually checked rather than automatically classified, add the answer about whether repairing makes migration easier (it doesn't), and then trigger the agent to apply these changes.

## Bottom line

**Keep GIL-10. Medium priority remains appropriate.** The last verified cloud state had no restore point or deletion guard.

The strongest current conclusion is that this risk remains open. However, expired `gcloud` authentication blocked a live cloud check today.

Moving development back to `~/clients` does not protect the VM. The local backup is hard-coded to `clients-pii-hardening`.

## Established facts

1. A 29 July cloud check found one 50 GB boot disk with:
   - No snapshots.
   - No snapshot policy.
   - Deletion protection disabled.
   - Automatic disk deletion enabled.

2. Production checks on 30 July confirmed that sessions, ownership records, and artifacts existed only on that VM.

3. GIL-10 has received no comments, status changes, or updates since creation.

4. I found no repository work or local `gcloud` command showing that anyone added protection afterwards.

5. The local Restic backup ran successfully today. Its configured source is only this local worktree.

They mostly agree.

The project ledger calls Restic an “Encrypted GCS recovery copy.” Its actual scope is narrower: the local worktree, not production.

The deploy guide explains how to rebuild a fresh stack. It does not provide a tested restore path for sessions or artifacts.

GIL-10 misses one important constraint. A whole boot-disk snapshot would preserve the identity table and recoverable blocks from earlier raw PII files.

The database, application code, and most infrastructure can be rebuilt. That process is manual and has not been tested as disaster recovery.

A VM deletion would probably erase:

- Ran’s conversation history.
- Feedback and ownership records.
- Agent-created CSVs, charts, and other artifacts.

This is not an active outage or evidence of a breach. It is a single-point-of-failure with a growing business-history loss.

## What would close GIL-10

1. Reauthenticate `gcloud` and repeat the live cloud checks.

2. Enable VM deletion protection as the immediate guard.

3. Define the VM state that must survive:
   - `/opt/avidor/sessions/`, including feedback and ownership records.
   - `/opt/avidor/workdir/.artifacts/`.
   - Any nightly outputs that Avidor wants to retain historically.

4. Back up only that state to encrypted, retained storage.

5. Exclude rebuildable twins, the identity table, raw files, and deployed code.

6. Restore the backup into a clean location and verify session and artifact recovery.

**Do not close the ticket after only enabling deletion protection.** That prevents one deletion path but does not provide recovery from disk failure or corruption.

## Bottom line

**Keep GIL-10. Medium priority remains appropriate.** The last verified cloud state had no restore point or deletion guard.

The strongest current conclusion is that this risk remains open. However, expired `gcloud` authentication blocked a live cloud check today.

Moving development back to `~/clients` does not protect the VM. The local backup is hard-coded to `clients-pii-hardening`.

## Established facts

1. A 29 July cloud check found one 50 GB boot disk with:
   - No snapshots.
   - No snapshot policy.
   - Deletion protection disabled.
   - Automatic disk deletion enabled.

2. Production checks on 30 July confirmed that sessions, ownership records, and artifacts existed only on that VM.

3. GIL-10 has received no comments, status changes, or updates since creation.

4. I found no repository work or local `gcloud` command showing that anyone added protection afterwards.

5. The local Restic backup ran successfully today. Its configured source is only this local worktree.

6. The public front door still redirects unauthenticated users to Google today. This confirms IAP still fails closed, not the VM state.

## Where the sources disagree

They mostly agree.

The project ledger calls Restic an “Encrypted GCS recovery copy.” Its actual scope is narrower: the local worktree, not production.

The deploy guide explains how to rebuild a fresh stack. It does not provide a tested restore path for sessions or artifacts.

GIL-10 misses one important constraint. A whole boot-disk snapshot would preserve the identity table and recoverable blocks from earlier raw PII files.

## Exposure today

The database, application code, and most infrastructure can be rebuilt. That process is manual and has not been tested as disaster recovery.

A VM deletion would probably erase:

- Ran’s conversation history.
- Feedback and ownership records.
- Agent-created CSVs, charts, and other artifacts.

This is not an active outage or evidence of a breach. It is a single-point-of-failure with a growing business-history loss.

## What would close GIL-10

1. Reauthenticate `gcloud` and repeat the live cloud checks.

2. Enable VM deletion protection as the immediate guard.

3. Define the VM state that must survive:
   - `/opt/avidor/sessions/`, including feedback and ownership records.
   - `/opt/avidor/workdir/.artifacts/`.
   - Any nightly outputs that Avidor wants to retain historically.

4. Back up only that state to encrypted, retained storage.

5. Exclude rebuildable twins, the identity table, raw files, and deployed code.

6. Restore the backup into a clean location and verify session and artifact recovery.

**Do not close the ticket after only enabling deletion protection.** That prevents one deletion path but does not provide recovery from disk failure or corruption.

## Could not verify

Expired `gcloud` authentication prevented verification of today’s snapshots, policies, deletion settings, disk settings, and VM contents.

I also could not rule out a change made through another computer or the Google Cloud console.

As of **2 August 2026, 16:29 IDT**, the production VM still has no cloud restore point. The earlier conclusion remains correct.

## Verified live

- `avidor-agent` is running with one 50 GB boot disk.
- VM deletion protection is off.
- The boot disk automatically deletes with the VM.
- The project has no snapshots or snapshot policies.
- It has no instant snapshots, machine images, or custom images.
- Google Backup and DR is not enabled.
- Conversation history and artifacts live on that boot disk.
- The disk currently holds:
  - 51 conversation log files.
  - 45 ownership records.
  - 37 artifact files.
  - No persisted feedback records.
- Conversation history changed today. Artifact files last changed on 30 July.
- These two state areas total only about 12 MB.
- I found no VM-state backup tool or scheduled backup job.
- The encrypted Restic backup still covers the local checkout only.

## Inferred from those facts

Deleting the VM would also delete its disk. Google Cloud currently has nothing from which to restore that disk.

The conversation logs, ownership records, and artifacts appear to be the only production copies. I cannot prove that nobody manually copied them elsewhere.

The feedback detail has changed. **There are no feedback records to lose today.** The existing conversation history and artifacts remain exposed.

## Questions that remain open

1. **Has anyone made a manual external copy?**  
   This project and VM show none. I cannot inspect unrelated computers, accounts, or GCP projects.

2. **How long must Ran’s history and files survive?**  
   The cloud cannot answer this business decision.

3. **How quickly must production recover?**  
   This decides whether state-only backup is enough, or whether Gilad also wants whole-disk recovery.

## Bottom line

**GIL-10 is still open and should leave Backlog.** This is an active single-copy risk, not an outdated ticket.

The proportionate fix is:

1. Enable VM deletion protection.
2. Stop the boot disk from auto-deleting.
3. Back up the small mutable state off-disk on a schedule.
4. Test restoring that state into a separate location.

A whole-disk snapshot is faster for full recovery. However, it also copies secrets and protected identity data. A narrow encrypted backup of the mutable state has a smaller security footprint.

I made no cloud, repository, or Linear changes.

GIL-10 came back, now checked against the live cloud rather than documents.

**It is real and still open.** The production machine runs on one disk. Deletion protection is off, the disk deletes automatically with the machine, and the project has no snapshots, no snapshot policy, no machine images, and no Google backup service enabled. Nothing exists to restore from.

**But it is far smaller than it sounded.** The data that exists only there totals about 12 MB: 51 conversation logs, 45 ownership records, and 37 artifact files. The conversation history changed today, so it is live and growing. This is not a heavy infrastructure problem. It is a small file-copy problem that nobody has set up yet.

One correction to what I told you earlier. I said Ran's feedback was among the things at risk. There are no feedback records on the disk at all, so there is nothing to lose there. The conversation history and the artifacts are the real exposure.

## The part that needs your judgment

The obvious fix is a whole-disk snapshot, and it is the wrong one here. A disk snapshot copies everything, including the secrets and the protected identity data. After the months you have spent narrowing where that data can live, a scheduled full-disk copy quietly widens it again. Backing up only the 12 MB of conversation and artifact state keeps the security footprint small.

That is a genuine trade. Whole-disk recovers production faster after a failure. Narrow backup protects what is irreplaceable without spreading the sensitive material.

Two questions only you can answer, and they decide the shape: how long must Ran's history survive, and how fast must production come back after a failure.

## What is free right now

Two settings cost nothing and close the most likely way this goes wrong: turn on deletion protection, and stop the disk from deleting with the machine. Neither is a backup, so neither closes the ticket, but together they remove the accident case. The scheduled copy and a tested restore are what actually close it.

Nothing here touches the migration. Say the word and I'll take the two free settings, or leave it entirely until you have decided the shape.
